text: A-R-A-G system that works on your test queries may fail catastrophically on user queries you did not anticipate. Systematic evaluation, not anecdotal testing, is what separates production ready systems from demos. In this lesson, R-A-G evaluation uses three metrics, faithfulness, answer relevance, and context recall. Faithfulness measures whether the generated answer is reported by the retrieved documents, a hallucination score. Answer relevance measures whether the answer addresses the question. Context recall measures whether the retrieved documents contain the information needed to answer the question correctly. The R-A-G-A-S framework retrieval augmented generation assessment automates all three metrics using an LLM evaluator. It takes your question answer context triples and scores them. Implementation. PIP install R-A-G-S, then score your system using evaluate with your test dataset. The most important metric in practice is faithfulness. An answer that is relevant but not supported by the retrieved documents is a hallucination, which is worse than no answer. Target faithfulness above 0.85 before deployment. Answer relevance above 0.80 is acceptable. Context recall below 0.70 means your retrieval is failing, fixed retrieval before fixing generation, improvement strategies. One, if context recall is low, improve chunking strategy, add hybrid search, or use a re-ranker model. Two, if faithfulness is low, strengthen the system prompt to require citations, reduce the number of retrieved chunks, or use a more instruction following model. Three, if answer relevance is low, improve query understanding, add query expansion, generating multiple query variants before retrieval, or restructure documents. Four, if all metrics are low, the embedding model is likely a poor fit for your document language and vocabulary. Switch to a domain specific or multilingual model. R-A-G evaluation must be done on a representative test set. Queries that reflect real user behavior, not queries that developer wrote to demonstrate the system working. A developer writing test queries unconsciously avoids the edge cases that real users will hit. The best evaluation data sets are built from real user queries collected during a limited beta deployment. Test set quality determines evaluation reliability. A 100-question evaluation set built from real user queries is worth more than a 1000-question set built by the developer who knows the system's vocabulary. Remember this. Never write your own evaluation questions. Get them from real users, customer service staff, or domain experts who do not know your system's internal vocabulary. Apply what you learn in this lesson and you will see results immediately. Your skills bear fruit.
